cold

Type this into a chatbot: the capital of the state containing Dallas is. Press Enter. In the second before the answer appears, your sentence is chopped into about a dozen pieces, each piece becomes a long list of numbers, and those numbers pass through a tower of around a hundred layers. And researchers have now caught one of those layers lighting up with a single idea: Texas. Today we follow one sentence through the whole machine, and end on the part nobody fully understands.
cold

First, a warning about what this is not. It does not look anything up. There is no database of facts inside. There is one trick, repeated over and over: guess the next small piece of text. Then do it again. That is all a chatbot ever does. Everything else we are about to see exists to make that single guess a good one. And the first step is strange. Your words stop being words.
tokens

The model cannot read letters. It reads tokens, which are pieces of words. The method comes from a 2015 paper by Rico Sennrich and colleagues, called byte pair encoding. Start with single characters, then keep merging the pairs that appear together most often in a huge pile of text. Common words become one piece. Rare words get chopped up. GPT-2, published in 2019, ended up with a vocabulary of exactly fifty thousand, two hundred and fifty-seven pieces.
tokens

That is why a chatbot can stumble over counting the letters in strawberry. It never saw the letters. It saw a few pieces, each one just an ID number, like a coat check ticket. Our Dallas sentence becomes about a dozen tickets. But a ticket number tells the machine nothing. The number four thousand is not close to the number four thousand and one in meaning. So the next step has to give each ticket a meaning.
embed

Each ID is used to look up a long list of numbers, called an embedding. In GPT-3, published in 2020, every single token becomes twelve thousand, two hundred and eighty-eight numbers. Think of it as a position in a huge space. Words used in similar ways end up close together. Directions in that space can even carry meaning, which our Short on embeddings showed. Dallas lands near Houston. Texas lands near the other states. Meaning, turned into geometry.
embed

There is a catch. A list of numbers for each word says nothing about order. Dog bites man and man bites dog would look identical. So position gets mixed in too. The original 2017 design added waves of different lengths. Many newer models rotate the numbers instead, an idea from a 2021 paper. Now each token carries what it is and where it sits. But take the word bank. River bank, or bank account? That list of numbers is the same either way. Context has to flow in.
attn

The trick that makes context flow is called attention, from the 2017 paper Attention Is All You Need, by Ashish Vaswani and colleagues. Every token writes a question, called a query, and holds a label, called a key. The query is compared with every earlier key, the best matches get high scores, and the token then pulls in a weighted mix of what those earlier tokens carry, called their values.
attn

Take the sentence: the animal did not cross the street because it was too tired. What does it point to? Attention lets the token it look back and lean mostly toward animal. Not a spotlight on one word, but a weighted blend across many. And it only looks backward. A token is never allowed to peek at words that come after it, because the model is being trained to guess exactly those. If you were the model, what would you need to keep from the past?
attn

One attention calculation is not enough, so the model runs many in parallel, called heads. The original Transformer used eight. GPT-3 used ninety-six. Each head can learn to track something different, maybe grammar, maybe which noun a pronoun means. Their results are combined, and the token walks away knowing a little more about its surroundings. That is one step. It is not thinking yet. To get anywhere, you have to stack it.
tower

Attention is paired with a second part, a wide network that processes each token on its own. Together they form one block. The original Transformer stacked six blocks. GPT-3 stacked ninety-six, with one hundred and seventy-five billion adjustable numbers across the whole tower. Between blocks, a running copy of each token is passed along and gently edited, never replaced. Layer by layer, the numbers for the final token drift toward an answer.
tower

Where do the facts live? Nobody knows precisely, but evidence suggests a lot of them sit in those wide networks, like a vast, blurry memory. All of it was set by training: reading about three hundred billion tokens of text, guessing the next one, being nudged each time it was wrong, billions of times over. Now, one honest note. OpenAI has not published the design of the models inside ChatGPT today. Every number here comes from the published recipes. At the top of the tower, the output is not a word. It is a list of odds.
dice

The top of the tower gives a score to every one of those fifty thousand or more possible tokens. A function called softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Maybe Austin gets a very high share, then a few others, then a long tail of nonsense. Now the machine has a choice. It could always take the top one. That is called greedy decoding. If you had to pick every next word, would you always take the safest? A 2019 paper by Ari Holtzman and colleagues found that this gives bland, repetitive text.
dice

So instead, it rolls a weighted die. A setting called temperature, a term borrowed from a 2015 paper by Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues, reshapes the odds. Low temperature sharpens them toward the favourite. High temperature flattens them, so unlikely tokens get a real chance. It is not creativity, it is just how bold the die is. Another method, top p, cuts off the unreliable tail before rolling. One token is chosen. Austin.
dice

And then the whole thing starts again. The new token is added to the end of the sentence, and the entire tower runs once more to pick the next one. Then again. Every word you read from a chatbot is a fresh trip through every layer. That sounds painfully slow. And it would be, if the machine did not have one trick for remembering its own work.
cache

Look at what the second trip needs. The keys and values for every earlier token were already worked out on the first trip, and they have not changed. So the machine stores them. This is called the KV cache. Each new token only computes its own, and reads the rest from memory. It is like keeping your earlier calculations on the desk instead of redoing them from page one.
cache

The price is memory. The cache grows with every token in the conversation, which is one reason very long chats are expensive to run. A 2022 paper by Reiner Pope and colleagues studies exactly this trade-off between speed and memory. So now we have a machine that guesses one piece of text at a time, quickly. But a guesser that only continues text is not an assistant. Ask it a question and it might just continue with more questions.
assist

The missing step was shown in 2022 by a team led by Long Ouyang at OpenAI. First, people wrote examples of good answers. Then the model produced several answers, people ranked them from best to worst, and a method called reinforcement learning from human feedback pushed the model toward what people preferred. The result was striking. People preferred answers from a model with one point three billion adjustable numbers over the raw one hundred and seventy-five billion version.
end

So that is the journey of your sentence. Tokens, then embeddings, then attention, a tower of layers, a weighted die, and a cache, all repeated for every piece. It is simple enough to explain in ten minutes. Yet no one can fully explain why any single answer comes out the way it does. In 2025, researchers at Anthropic studying their own model traced the Dallas question and found an internal step for Texas before Austin. In poems, they found it picking rhyming words before writing the line.
end

So it writes one token at a time, yet it can plan ahead. The methods are partial, and they only show small pieces of what happens inside. But it means the machine is not merely guessing blindly. It is building something in there, and we are only beginning to read it. This is LATOON. Voyaging the Unseen.
